html:
Barotseland is the kingdom of the Lozi people on the upper Zambezi floodplain, in what is now western Zambia. The map shows it from 1783 to 1900.

The Lozi built their life around the river's yearly flood. They farmed and fished on the plain in the dry season and moved to higher ground when the water rose. The king, the Litunga, led the move each year in a royal barge, a ceremony still held today as the Kuomboka.

In the 1830s the Kololo, a Sotho people driven north by the wars of the Mfecane, conquered the kingdom. David Livingstone met their ruler Sebetwane in 1851. The Lozi rose and overthrew Kololo rule in 1864, but kept the Kololo language, which became Silozi.

King Lewanika, ruling from 1878, sought British protection against the Ndebele and Portuguese and signed concessions with the British South Africa Company in 1890. Barotseland became a protected kingdom within Northern Rhodesia, and joined independent Zambia in 1964. Its status within Zambia is still argued over.
